citations.quote: Let $\rho(z)=\max\{0,z\}$ and define $\tau(x)=2\rho(x)-4\rho(x-1/2)$ for $x\in[0,1]$. For each integer $q\ge0$, $\tau^q$ is affine and maps bijectively onto $[0,1]$ on each of the $2^q$ dyadic intervals $[j2^{-q},(j+1)2^{-q}]$, with slope of magnitude $2^q$. It is computed on $[0,1]$ by a ReLU network with $2q$ hidden units, $q$ hidden layers, and $O(q+1)$ weights; its depth, counting input and output layers, is $q+2$.

Let $L\ge0$, let $f:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ satisfy $|f(x)-f(y)|\le L|x-y|$, and let $N\ge1$ be an integer. The Bernstein polynomial $$B_Nf(x):=\sum_{j=0}^N f(j/N)\binom Njx^j(1-x)^{N-j}$$ satisfies $$\sup_{x\in[0,1]}|B_Nf(x)-f(x)|\le\frac{L}{2\sqrt N}.$$

derivations.claim: On $[0,1]$, $h(x)=2x$ for $x\le1/2$ and $h(x)=2-2x$ for $x\ge1/2$, so it equals the tent map in [F1], maps the interval into itself, and is $2$-Lipschitz. Thus $h^5$ is $32$-Lipschitz. For $N=2^{22}$, [F2] gives a degree-$N$ polynomial $P_N$ with $\sup_{[0,1]}|h^5-P_N|\le32/(2\sqrt N)=1/128$.

A single gate with the constant predicate polynomial $q_1(z)=1$, condition $q_1(z)\ge0$, and polynomial piece $P_N$ is $(1,1,N)$-semi-algebraic; the predicate is always true and has degree $0$. Since $2^{1/N}<2$, the allowed integer node count is one. The normalized Lebesgue integral on $[0,1]$ of its error is at most $1/128<1/64$, so this is a counterexample to the claimed uniform lower bound.

The gate $P_N(z)=B_N(h^5)(z)$ is a single $(1,1,N)$-semi-algebraic gate: use the constant predicate polynomial $q_1(z)=1$ with condition $q_1(z)\ge0$, and the one polynomial piece $p_1(z)=P_N(z)$, whose degree is at most $N$. citations.quote: Fix integers $d,r\ge1$. A ReLU feedforward network from $[0,1]^d$ to $\mathbb R^r$ is a finite acyclic feedforward computation graph with $d$ input coordinates, hidden units applying $\rho(z)=\max\{0,z\}$ to affine combinations of earlier unit values, and $r$ affine output units. Edges may skip layers. Its depth is the maximum number of layers met on an input-to-output path, counting the input and output layers, so a network with one hidden layer has depth $3$. Its computation units are its hidden and output units; its connections are its directed weighted edges; its weights are all connection coefficients and unit biases. The number of each quantity counts scalar entries, including zero entries only when the architecture explicitly includes them. A layered fully connected ReLU network is the specialization in which edges join consecutive layers and every such edge is present.

Let $k,m,d\ge1$ be integers and let $p_1,\ldots,p_m$ be real polynomials in $k$ variables, each of total degree at most $d$ (including the zero polynomial). The number of strict sign vectors $(\operatorname{sgn}p_1(x),\ldots,\operatorname{sgn}p_m(x))\in\{-1,1\}^m$ attained at points where all polynomials are nonzero is at most $(2md+1)^k$. The number of binary vectors $(\mathbf1_{p_i(x)>0})_{i=1}^m$ is also at most $(2md+1)^k$, and the same bound holds with $\ge0$ in place of $>0$. The number of ternary sign vectors in $\{-1,0,1\}^m$ is at most $(4md+1)^k$. Each assertion remains valid when $x$ is restricted to any subset of $\mathbb R^k$.

Let $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$ be a family of subsets of an arbitrary set $X$. For a finite $T\subseteq X$, its trace is

$$\mathcal C|_T:=\{C\cap T:C\in\mathcal C\}.$$

The family $\mathcal C$ **shatters** $T$ when $\mathcal C|_T=\mathcal P(T)$. This extends the finite-ground-set trace convention of [[def-shattering-and-vc-dimension]]: any finite $T$ can be relabeled by $[|T|]$, and relabeling preserves all traces and their cardinalities.

For a nonempty class, its **VC dimension** $d(\mathcal C)$ is the greatest size of a finite shattered set if those sizes are bounded, is $0$ if no singleton is shattered, and is $+\infty$ if finite shattered sets have unbounded size. When the dimension is finite, its **VC index** is

$$V(\mathcal C):=d(\mathcal C)+1,$$

equivalently the least positive integer $V$ such that no $V$-point subset is shattered. The empty class is assigned $V=0$ by convention and is treated separately in the entropy theorem.

derivations.claim: Remove all hidden units that have no path to the output. Also remove all hidden units having no input ancestor: for each fixed parameter assignment their values are constants in $x$, and their contributions to a remaining unit or the output can be added to its existing bias. Allowing these new biases to vary independently produces a fixed reduced architecture whose realization class contains the original class. No new coefficient slots are needed, because every surviving computation unit already has a bias; edges and removed units only disappear. If the output has no input ancestor, the original class consists of constant functions and has VC dimension at most $1$, which satisfies the conclusions. Otherwise the reduced graph has $w\le W$ counted slots, $U$ hidden units, and $U+1\le w$ because the output and every hidden unit have counted biases. Every remaining unit lies on an input-to-output path. Rank each hidden unit by the maximum number of computation units on an input-to-that-unit path, and give the output its analogous rank $K$. Then each edge increases rank, and $K\le L-1$ and $K\le U+1\le w$. Empty ranks can be omitted. It suffices to bound the reduced class.

Fix arbitrary sample points $x_1,\ldots,x_m$. For any prescribed binary mask $b\in\{0,1\}^U$, replace the ReLU at hidden unit $v$ by multiplication of its preactivation by $b_v$. Its preactivation and the final output are now polynomials in the $w$ parameters. By induction along the graph, a unit of rank $j$ has polynomial degree at most $j$: input values have degree zero, multiplication by an edge coefficient raises degree by one, addition of a bias has degree one, and multiplication by a fixed mask entry changes no degree. Thus every such polynomial has degree at most $K\le w$. On any actual parameter vector the convention $b_v=\mathbf1_{z_v>0}$ gives a unique mask, even when a preactivation is zero, and the masked polynomials then reproduce every actual unit value.

For each sample point and each of the $2^U$ masks, form the $U$ preactivation polynomials and the output polynomial minus $a$. There are $M=m(U+1)2^U$ polynomials, all of degree at most $w$. Their strict-positivity vector determines the actual output classification at every sample point: evaluate units in topological order, determining their actual mask by the relevant preactivation entry, then read the output entry for that mask. Hence the number of label vectors is at most $(2Mw+1)^w\le(3mw^2 2^w)^w$ by [F2]. If the classifier uses $\ge a$, take the hidden-unit mask $\mathbf1_{z_v\ge0}$ and use nonnegativity vectors throughout; at zero, multiplying by either mask value still gives the ReLU value, so the same count holds.

For a second count, start with the single parameter-space cell $\mathbb R^w$. At stage $j$, refine every existing cell by the activation bits of all units of rank $j$ at all $m$ sample points; at the final stage refine by the output threshold bits. Within a cell, all earlier mask bits are fixed, so the relevant $mN_j$ preactivation polynomials, or output-minus-threshold polynomials, have degree at most $j\le K$ by step 2.1, where $N_j$ is the number of units at that rank, with $N_K=1$ for the output. By [F2] there are at most $(2mN_jK+1)^w\le(3mwK)^w$ refinements of each cell. This estimate holds on an arbitrary cell; no connectedness or openness is needed. After $K$ stages, the number of cells, hence the number of output label vectors, is at most $(3mwK)^{wK}$. The construction using $\ge0$ activation bits and nonnegativity output bits proves the identical bound for the other threshold convention.

Put $m_0=64w^2$. At this sample size the base-two logarithm of the last bound is $w(\log_2 3+\log_2m_0+2\log_2w+w)=w(w+\log_2 3+6+4\log_2w)\le13w^2<m_0$, using $\log_2w\le w$ for integers $w\ge1$. Thus no $m_0$-point set can be shattered, and [F3] rules out all larger shattered sets. Consequently $\operatorname{VC}(\mathcal H_a)<64w^2\le64W^2$.

Write $A=wK$ and $B=\log_2(2w)\ge1$, and take the integer $m_1=\lceil64AB\rceil\le65AB$. Since $K\le w$, one has $\log_2 A\le2\log_2w$ and $\log_2B\le B$. The base-two logarithm of the label-count bound at $m=m_1$ is at most $A\log_2(195A^2B)\le A(8+4\log_2w+\log_2B)\le A(4+5B)\le9AB< m_1$. No set of $m_1$ points is shattered. Therefore $\operatorname{VC}(\mathcal H_a)<m_1\le65wK\log_2(2w)\le65WL\log_2(2W)$. Conversion between logarithm bases changes only an absolute constant. For $W\ge2$, $\log(2W)\le2\log W$ and $L\ge1$, so this implies the requested $CL^2W\log W$ estimate. Together with step 4.1 and the constant-output case, this proves every assertion.

citations.quote:
Assume AC. Infinite real projective space has
$$H^*(\mathbb {RP}^{\infty};\mathbb F_2)\cong\mathbb F_2[a],\qquad |a|=1.$$

For every integer $n\geq0$, restriction along the standard skeletal inclusion
$i_n:\mathbb {RP}^n\hookrightarrow\mathbb {RP}^{\infty}$ is an isomorphism in
degrees at most $n$. For $n\geq1$ it sends $a$ to the unique nonzero
degree-one class on $\mathbb {RP}^n$; for $n=0$ it sends $a$ to zero.

For each integer $m\ge0$, $\mathbb{RP}^m=S^m/(x\sim-x)$ has a CW structure with one cell in each dimension $0,\ldots,m$. Orientations can be chosen so its integral cellular complex has $C_j=\mathbb Z$ in these degrees, $d_j=2$ for positive even $j$, and $d_j=0$ for odd $j$. Consequently its integral homology is $\mathbb Z$ in degree zero, $\mathbb Z/2$ in odd degrees $0<j<m$, $\mathbb Z$ in degree $j=m$ when $m$ is odd, and zero otherwise. For $m=0$ only the degree-zero copy occurs.

The quotient $q:\mathbb{RP}^2\to\mathbb{RP}^2/\mathbb{RP}^1\cong S^2$ induces an isomorphism $H_2(\mathbb{RP}^2;\mathbb F_2)\to H_2(S^2;\mathbb F_2)$. Assuming AC, it therefore induces an isomorphism $q^*:H^2(S^2;\mathbb F_2)\to H^2(\mathbb{RP}^2;\mathbb F_2)$, both groups being $\mathbb F_2$.

Assume AC. Let $X$ be a nonempty finite CW complex of dimension $d$, and let
$R$ be a commutative ring. For every $n>d$ the singular cohomology vanishes:
$$H^n(X;R)=0.$$
More generally, for a CW pair $(X,A)$ with $X$ finite of dimension $d$ one has
$H^n(X,A;R)=0$ for every $n>d$.
If $f,g:X\to Y$ are homotopic continuous maps, then $f^*=g^*:H^n(Y;G)\to H^n(X;G)$ for every integer $n$ and every abelian coefficient group $G$.

For continuous $f:X\to Y$ and a commutative unital ring $R$, pullback on singular cohomology satisfies
$$f^*(a\smile b)=f^*a\smile f^*b,\qquad f^*(1)=1.$$
Cup product is associative already on cochains. Consequently $f^*:H^*(Y;R)\to H^*(X;R)$ is a unital graded-ring homomorphism. Homotopic maps give the same homomorphism.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: We first rule out a continuous odd map $g:S^m\to S^{m-1}$ for $m\ge1$. Such a map descends to $b:\mathbb{RP}^m\to\mathbb{RP}^{m-1}$, $b([x])=[g(x)]$. This is continuous by the quotient topology, since the composite with the sphere quotient is continuous and $g(-x)=-g(x)$.

In the coordinate subspace $\mathbb R^{m+1}\oplus\mathbb R^m\subset\mathbb R^{\infty}$, define $$H([x],t)=[\cos(\pi t/2)x,\ \sin(\pi t/2)g(x)],\qquad 0\le t\le1.$$ Its representing vector has norm one. Replacing $x$ by $-x$ negates the whole vector, so the projective point is independent of representative. Continuity can be checked on each chart where a chosen coordinate of $x$ is nonzero: choose the unit representative with that coordinate positive, which varies continuously in the ratios of the remaining coordinates, and use the displayed formula. These charts cover projective space, proving joint continuity in $([x],t)$. Thus $H$ is a homotopy from $i_m$ to $j\circ b$, where $j([y])=[0,y]$ is the inclusion in the second block. The same formula with $y$ in the first $m$ coordinates and $y$ in the second block, namely $[\cos(\pi t/2)y,0,\sin(\pi t/2)y]$, is a homotopy from $i_{m-1}$ to $j$. Both homotopies lie in the finite projective subspace $\mathbb{RP}^{2m}$ of the infinite space and therefore are continuous there as well.

Put $a_k=i_k^*a$. By [F3] and step 2.1, $a_m=b^*a_{m-1}$, including $m=1$ when $a_0=0$. Consequently $$a_m^m=b^*(a_{m-1}^m)=0,$$ since $H^m(\mathbb{RP}^{m-1};\mathbb F_2)=0$ by [F2]. On the other hand, [F1] says $a^m\ne0$ and that $i_m^*$ is an isomorphism in degree $m$, so $a_m^m=i_m^*(a^m)\ne0$. These incompatible conclusions rule out every such odd map.

For $m\ge1$, if $h(x)-h(-x)$ never vanished, then $$g(x)=\frac{h(x)-h(-x)}{\|h(x)-h(-x)\|_2}$$ would be continuous, take values in $S^{m-1}$ and satisfy $g(-x)=-g(x)$. Step 3.1 rules this out, so an antipodal pair has equal images. When $m=0$, the codomain $\mathbb R^0$ consists of one point and the two points of $S^0$ have equal images directly. AC is inherited exactly as stated in [A1].

citations.quote:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For every integer $m\ge0$ and every continuous map $h:S^m\to\mathbb R^m$, there exists $x\in S^m$ with $h(x)=h(-x)$. Here $S^m$ is the Euclidean unit sphere in $\mathbb R^{m+1}$.

derivations.claim: Define $p(t)=(4t(1-t))^{n+1}$ for $0\le t\le1$ and $p(t)=0$ otherwise, and put $\psi(x)=\prod_{r=1}^d p(x_r)$. The one-sided derivatives of $p$ of orders $0,\ldots,n$ vanish at each endpoint because the polynomial has a zero of multiplicity $n+1$ there. Hence the zero extension is $C^n(\mathbb R)$, and $\psi\in C^n(\mathbb R^d)$ is supported in $[0,1]^d$, is one at its center, and lies between zero and one. Set $$B=\max_{|\alpha|\le n}\|D^\alpha\psi\|_\infty\ge1.$$ This is finite since the derivatives are continuous polynomials on the compact cube and zero outside it. Their classical derivatives are weak derivatives: integrate by parts successively in each coordinate against a compactly supported smooth test function; endpoint terms vanish because the derivatives below order $n$ match their zero extensions. This also verifies the weak derivative identity after every scaling and finite sum used below.

Set $N=W+1$ and $k=\lceil N^{1/d}\rceil$. Partition $Q$ into $k^d$ closed coordinate cubes of side $1/k$, and take the first $N$ in lexicographic order. Write $v_j$ for their lower vertices and put $$\phi_j(x)=B^{-1}k^{-n}\psi(k(x-v_j)),\qquad j=1,\ldots,N.$$ Distinct supports have disjoint interiors; all derivatives of orders at most $n$ vanish on their boundaries. Thus, for $u=(u_1,\ldots,u_N)\in[-1,1]^N$, the sum $T(u)=\sum_j u_j\phi_j$ satisfies $\|D^\alpha T(u)\|_\infty\le B^{-1}k^{|\alpha|-n}\|D^\alpha\psi\|_\infty\le1$. The weak derivative verification in step 1.1 proves $T(u)\in F_{d,n}$. Disjoint interiors, and evaluation at the centers, give the exact identity $$\|T(u)\|_\infty=B^{-1}k^{-n}\max_j|u_j|.$$ In particular $T$ is linear, odd and continuous into $C(Q)$ with its uniform norm.

For $z\in S^{N-1}=S^W$, put $R(z)=z/\|z\|_\infty$. Its denominator is nonzero, and $R$ is continuous and odd with $\|R(z)\|_\infty=1$. Therefore $z\mapsto M(T(R(z)))$ is continuous into $\mathbb R^W$. By [F2], some antipodal pair has equal images. Setting $f=T(R(z))$, we obtain $M(f)=M(-f)$ and $\|f\|_\infty=B^{-1}k^{-n}$.

Let $q=\eta(M(f))=\eta(M(-f))$. The triangle inequality yields $$2B^{-1}k^{-n}=\|f-(-f)\|_\infty\le\|f-q\|_\infty+\|-f-q\|_\infty.$$ At least one of the two errors is at least $B^{-1}k^{-n}$. Because $k\le2N^{1/d}$, this is at least $c_{d,n}N^{-n/d}$ with $c_{d,n}=2^{-n}B^{-1}>0$. This proves the asserted supremum bound without any regularity of $\eta$.

If every error is at most $\varepsilon$, step 4.1 gives $W+1\ge(c_{d,n}/\varepsilon)^{d/n}$. Since $W\ge1$ implies $W+1\le2W$, we obtain $W\ge\tfrac12 c_{d,n}^{d/n}\varepsilon^{-d/n}$. The construction works at $W=1$, $d=1$, $n=1$, on cubes touching the boundary and when $N=k^d$, with exactly the same vanishing-derivative argument. AC is inherited from [F2] and subsumes the countable choice in [F1]; choosing finitely many indexed cubes or derivatives introduces no new choice principle.

derivations.claim: A computational block with two gates $\rho(z)$, $\rho(z-1/2)$ followed by the gate $\rho(2u-4v)$ computes $h$. Compose $q$ blocks, identifying repeated parameter slots. Only the coordinate-selection vector of length $d$ and the four scalar slots $0,-1/2,2,-4$ are needed: the first vector supplies coefficient $1$ for the selected coordinate and coefficient $0$ for the others, and its selected coefficient $1$ may also supply the fixed unit coefficient in subsequent blocks. There are $3q$ gates and $2q$ computational layers. Appending an affine identity produces the stated conversion. On the cube the output is the tent iterate in [F1].

Fix all coordinates except $x_1=z$, and consider any comparator with actual nonempty layer widths $m_1,\ldots,m_\ell$ and $\ell\le k$, $\sum_i m_i\le m$. Maintain one common partition of the line into open intervals on which all gates through layer $i$ are polynomials of degree at most $\beta^i$. Initially there is one interval and input coordinates are affine. In one previous interval, each of the at most $tm_i$ gate predicates at layer $i$ is a polynomial of degree at most $\alpha\beta^{i-1}$ after substitution, hence introduces at most that many roots unless identically zero, in which case its test is constant. Thus the new common partition has at most $1+tm_i\alpha\beta^{i-1}$ pieces per old piece. On each piece all indicators are constant, and the gate output is a polynomial of degree at most $\beta^i$. Skip edges cause no change: earlier outputs already have polynomial degree at most $\beta^{i-1}$ on this common partition.

It follows that the threshold classifier $1[g(z)\ge1/2]$ is constant on at most $C=(1+\beta^\ell)\prod_{i=1}^{\ell}(1+tm_i\alpha\beta^{i-1})$ open intervals. Identically zero threshold polynomials contribute no roots. Since every factor's nonconstant term is at least one, $C\le2(2t\alpha)^\ell\beta^{\ell(\ell+1)/2}\prod_i m_i\le2(2t\alpha m/\ell)^\ell\beta^{\ell(\ell+1)/2}\le B$, where the penultimate inequality is AM–GM. The same partition argument applies for every fixed offset of the remaining coordinates.

Put $T=2^q$. By [F1], the target threshold classifier alternates on $N=T+1$ intervals in $[0,1]$. Its two end intervals have length $1/(2T)$ and each of the others length $1/T$. The integral of $|f-1/2|$ is $1/(8T)$ on each end interval and $1/(4T)$ on each other interval. A comparator classifier with at most $C$ intervals has at most $C-1$ internal boundaries. Discard target intervals containing such a boundary. At most $C-1$ intervals are discarded; in each of the at most $C$ remaining runs the alternating target labels disagree with the constant comparator on at least half the run length minus $1/2$. Hence at least $(N-2C)/2$ target intervals disagree throughout, whenever this quantity is positive. Their contribution gives $\int_0^1|f-g|\,dz\ge\max\{0,(N-2C)/(16T)\}$. Endpoint equalities have no effect on the integral. Integrating in the other coordinates gives the displayed bound and its $B\le T/4$ consequence.

Write $s=t\alpha\beta$. For $\ell=1$, the bound in step 2.1 is $4sm$. For $\ell\ge2$, use $(2/\ell)^\ell\le1$, $\ell(\ell+1)/2\le\ell^2$, and $\ell\le\ell^2$ to bound it by $2(sm)^{\ell^2}$. Therefore $B\le4(sm)^{k^2}$. If $m\le2^{k/s}$ and $s2^{k/s}\le2^k$, then $B\le2^{k^3+2}=T/4$. For $s=1$ the condition is equality; for fixed $s>1$ it is equivalent to $k\ge s\log_2(s)/(s-1)$, so it eventually holds. This proves the exponential-budget assertion with all its indicated parameter cases.

A binary decision tree with $r$ total nodes has at most $(r-1)/2$ internal branch nodes. On a fixed line each nonconstant affine test has at most one zero. A sum of at most $t$ such trees, with $r\le2^{A/t}$ and $A=k^3$, is constant away from at most $t(2^{A/t}-1)/2$ thresholds. Convexity of $u\mapsto2^u$ yields $t(2^{A/t}-1)\le2^A-1$ for $t\ge1$. Thus its threshold classifier has at most $(2^A+1)/2\le2^{A+2}=T/4$ intervals. Step 3.1 proves the tree assertion. Finally at $k=d=t=\alpha=1$, the target $h^5$ is $32$-Lipschitz; its degree-$2^{22}$ Bernstein polynomial has uniform error at most $32/(2\sqrt{2^{22}})=1/128$ by [F2]. This polynomial is one $(1,1,2^{22})$ gate, allowed by the node budget $2^{1/2^{22}}>1$, so the parameter restriction cannot be omitted.

citations.quote:
Let $F$ be a field. Every polynomial in the iterated ring
$F[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ has a unique finite expansion

$$f=\sum_{\mathbf{t}}c_{\mathbf{t}}x^{\mathbf{t}},\qquad x^{\mathbf{t}}:=x_1^{t_1}\cdots x_n^{t_n},$$

over finitely many multi-indices $\mathbf{t}=(t_1,\dots,t_n)\in\mathbb{N}^n$.

For such an index, the scalar $c_{\mathbf{t}}$ is the **coefficient**
$[x^{\mathbf{t}}]f$ of the monomial $x^{\mathbf{t}}$.

The **degree in $x_i$** is the largest $t_i$ with $c_{\mathbf{t}}\ne0$, and the
**total degree** is the largest value of $t_1+\cdots+t_n$ with
$c_{\mathbf{t}}\ne0$. For the zero polynomial, every degree is left undefined.

Evaluation at a point $(a_1,\dots,a_n)\in F^n$ is the iterated substitution
supplied by the universal property of the polynomial ring.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty. The following are equivalent.

1. $A$ is compact.
2. $A$ is closed and bounded.
3. $A$ is pseudocompact.
4. Every continuous $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$ attains a maximum and a minimum on $A$.

This theorem is a ZF statement. The nonemptiness hypothesis is necessary for condition 4, because the empty image has neither a maximum nor a minimum.
If $f:U\subseteq\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R$ is differentiable at an interior local maximum or minimum $a$, then $\nabla f(a)=0$.

derivations.claim: First establish an elementary zero-counting fact. If $D\ge1$ and $r_i(x)=x_i^D+s_i(x)$ with $\deg s_i<D$ for $1\le i\le k$, then these $k$ polynomials have at most $D^k$ distinct common real zeros. In the quotient vector space $V=\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_k]/(r_1,\ldots,r_k)$, every monomial is a linear combination of the $D^k$ monomials $x_1^{a_1}\cdots x_k^{a_k}$ with $0\le a_i<D$. Indeed, if some exponent is at least $D$, replace its factor $x_i^D$ by $-s_i$ modulo the ideal. Every resulting monomial has strictly smaller total degree, so induction on total degree terminates and proves the spanning assertion. Thus $\dim V\le D^k$.

If no strict sign vector occurs, its bound is immediate. Otherwise choose one representative $a_\sigma$ for each attained strict vector $\sigma$. Only finitely many choices are involved, since there are at most $2^m$ vectors. Set $P=\prod_{i=1}^m p_i$ and $D=2md+1$. Then $P(a_\sigma)\ne0$. Choose a single $\delta>0$ so small that $H(a_\sigma)>0$ for every representative, where $H(x)=P(x)^2-\delta\sum_{i=1}^k x_i^{D+1}$. Such a choice exists: there are finitely many positive numbers $P(a_\sigma)^2$, and the other term has a fixed finite value at each representative. Since $D+1$ is even and greater than $2\deg P$, $H(x)\to-\infty$ as $\|x\|\to\infty$. Explicitly, $|P(x)|^2\le C(1+\|x\|^{2md})$ and $\sum_i x_i^{D+1}\ge k^{-(D+1)/2}\|x\|^{D+1}$.

For any finite list of distinct common zeros $z_1,\ldots,z_t$, evaluation defines a surjective linear map $V\to\mathbb R^t$. To see surjectivity, for every ordered pair $j\ne h$ choose a coordinate $i(j,h)$ in which $z_j$ and $z_h$ differ, and set $h_j(x)=\prod_{h\ne j}(x_{i(j,h)}-(z_h)_{i(j,h)})/((z_j)_{i(j,h)}-(z_h)_{i(j,h)})$. Then $h_j(z_h)$ is $1$ for $h=j$ and $0$ otherwise. Evaluation vanishes on the ideal because all its generators vanish at these zeros, so it is well defined on $V$ and the classes of $h_j$ map onto the standard coordinate vectors. Consequently $t\le\dim V\le D^k$. If there were more than $D^k$ zeros, choosing a finite list of $D^k+1$ of them would contradict this inequality. This proves the zero-counting fact without a genericity or multiplicity assumption.

For an attained strict vector $\sigma$, put $S_\sigma=\{x:\operatorname{sgn}p_i(x)=\sigma_i\text{ for all }i\}$. This is open. Its closure has a maximum of $H$: choose a closed ball containing $a_\sigma$ outside which $H<0$, and apply [F2] to its nonempty closed bounded intersection with $\overline{S_\sigma}$. The resulting maximum is positive, because $H(a_\sigma)>0$, and it is also the maximum over the full closure. Any point in $\overline{S_\sigma}\setminus S_\sigma$ has $p_i=0$ for some $i$ by continuity, so there $H=-\delta\sum_i x_i^{D+1}\le0$. Therefore the positive maximum is attained at a point $b_\sigma\in S_\sigma$, which is an interior local maximum of $H$. Distinct strict vectors give distinct such points.

By [F3] every $b_\sigma$ is a common zero of the $k$ polynomials $\partial_i H=2P\partial_iP-\delta(D+1)x_i^D$. After division by the nonzero coefficient $-\delta(D+1)$, each has the form $x_i^D+s_i(x)$ with $\deg s_i\le2md-1<D$. The zero-counting fact therefore bounds their distinct common zeros, and hence the number of strict sign vectors, by $D^k=(2md+1)^k$.

For binary vectors with $>0$, choose one representative per attained vector. Choose $\varepsilon>0$ smaller than every nonzero $|p_i|$ occurring at these finitely many representatives; if there are no such values, choose any positive $\varepsilon$. The strict signs of $p_i-\varepsilon$ at the representatives now encode their original binary vectors: positive values remain positive, and nonpositive values become negative. Applying the strict bound to the $m$ shifted polynomials gives the binary bound. For $\ge0$, use $p_i+\varepsilon$: nonnegative values become positive, and negative values remain negative. For ternary vectors choose representatives and $\varepsilon$ in the same way, and use the $2m$ polynomials $p_i-\varepsilon,p_i+\varepsilon$. Their strict sign pairs are $(-,-)$, $(-,+)$, and $(+,+)$ for the original negative, zero, and positive values, respectively, so distinct ternary vectors give distinct strict vectors. The strict bound with $2m$ polynomials gives $(4md+1)^k$. Restriction of the domain only removes vectors.

citations.quote: Let a scalar-input ReLU network have $H\ge0$ hidden layers of widths $n_1,\ldots,n_H$ and an affine output. On any interval, its output is affine on at most $\prod_{\ell=1}^H(n_\ell+1)$ subintervals. In particular, if it has $U=\sum_\ell n_\ell$ hidden units, the number of affine intervals is at most $(1+U/H)^H$ for $H\ge1$, and is $1$ when $H=0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d,n\ge1$ be integers, $Q=[0,1]^d$, and let $F_{d,n}\subset C(Q;\mathbb R)$ consist of the continuous functions whose restrictions represent members of $W^{n,\infty}((0,1)^d)$ satisfying
$$\max_{|\alpha|\le n}\|D^\alpha f\|_{L^\infty((0,1)^d)}\le1.$$
There exists $c_{d,n}>0$ such that, for every integer $W\ge1$, every map $\eta:\mathbb R^W\to C(Q;\mathbb R)$, and every map $M:F_{d,n}\to\mathbb R^W$ continuous for the uniform norm on $F_{d,n}$,
$$\sup_{f\in F_{d,n}}\|f-\eta(M(f))\|_\infty\ge c_{d,n}(W+1)^{-n/d}.$$
No continuity or measurability assumption is imposed on $\eta$. In particular, if this supremum is at most $\varepsilon>0$, then $W\ge C_{d,n}\varepsilon^{-d/n}$ for some $C_{d,n}>0$ depending only on $d,n$.

Fix a scalar-output ReLU feedforward architecture on $[0,1]^d$, permitting skip edges, with $W\ge1$ scalar connection coefficients and unit biases, and depth at most $L$. Fix a real threshold $a$. For its realizations $f_\theta$, let $\mathcal H_a=\{\{x:f_\theta(x)>a\}:\theta\in\mathbb R^W\}$. There is an absolute constant $C$ such that $\operatorname{VC}(\mathcal H_a)\le CW^2$ and $\operatorname{VC}(\mathcal H_a)\le CW L\log(2W)$. In particular, for $W\ge2$ the bound $\operatorname{VC}(\mathcal H_a)\le C L^2W\log W$ holds. The same assertions hold for $f_\theta(x)\ge a$. The parameter count includes every hidden and output bias, even when its chosen value is zero.

derivations.claim: By [F2], the hypotheses of clause (i) imply $\varepsilon\ge c_{d,n}(W+1)^{-n/d}$. Since $W\ge1$, we have $W+1\le2W$, hence $W\ge\tfrac12 c_{d,n}^{d/n}\varepsilon^{-d/n}$. The decoder needs no continuity; exactly the selector topology in the statement is used.

For clause (ii), write $p(t)=(4t(1-t))^{n+1}$ on $[0,1]$, extended by zero, and $\psi(x)=\prod_{r=1}^d p(x_r)$. The polynomial has endpoint zeros of order $n+1$, so its zero extension is $C^n$. Put $B=\max_{|\alpha|\le n}\|D^\alpha\psi\|_\infty\ge1$. Partition the cube into $K^d$ cubes of side $1/K$, with lower vertices $v_j$, and define $\phi_j(x)=B^{-1}K^{-n}\psi(K(x-v_j))$. All derivatives through order $n$ vanish at support boundaries, so the weak derivatives of these finite sums are their classical derivatives, as follows by integration by parts with zero boundary terms. Disjoint support interiors imply that every $f_\sigma=\sum_{j=1}^{K^d}\sigma_j\phi_j$, $\sigma_j\in\{-1,1\}$, belongs to $F_{d,n}$, since $\|D^\alpha f_\sigma\|_\infty\le K^{|\alpha|-n}\le1$ for $|\alpha|\le n$. At the center $x_j$ of cube $j$, $f_\sigma(x_j)=\sigma_jB^{-1}K^{-n}$.

For clause (iii), nonlinearity of $f$ implies that its Hessian is nonzero at an interior point; otherwise all first derivatives are constant on the connected cube and $f$ is affine. A symmetric nonzero Hessian has a direction with nonzero second directional derivative. By continuity choose a short interior segment and parameterize it by $t\in[0,1]$, so $g(t)=f(a+tv)$ has either $g''\ge c_0>0$ throughout or $g''\le-c_0<0$ throughout. The approximating network restricts to a scalar-input network of at most the same depth and unit count.

For sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$, choose $K=\lfloor(1/(4B\varepsilon))^{1/n}\rfloor\ge\tfrac12(1/(4B\varepsilon))^{1/n}$. Then the center amplitude $B^{-1}K^{-n}$ is at least $4\varepsilon$. Every approximant to $f_\sigma$ within $\varepsilon$ has positive output at centers with $\sigma_j=1$ and negative output at centers with $\sigma_j=-1$. Thus the threshold classifiers from the one fixed architecture shatter these $K^d\ge c_{d,n}\varepsilon^{-d/n}$ centers.

Combining step 2.1 with the first bound in [F3] gives $c_{d,n}\varepsilon^{-d/n}\le CW^2$, hence $W\ge c\varepsilon^{-d/(2n)}$. Shrinking the constant covers the remaining non-small accuracies, because any scalar-output architecture has $W\ge1$.

If $L\le c_1(\log(1/\varepsilon))^p$, the second bound in [F3] gives $c_{d,n}\varepsilon^{-d/n}\le Cc_1^2W(\log(1/\varepsilon))^{2p}\log(2W)$. For sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, if $W\ge\varepsilon^{-d/n}$ the desired conclusion follows directly since $\log(1/\varepsilon)\ge1$. Otherwise $\log(2W)\le\log2+(d/n)\log(1/\varepsilon)\le C_{d,n}\log(1/\varepsilon)$, and rearrangement gives $W\ge c_2\varepsilon^{-d/n}(\log(1/\varepsilon))^{-2p-1}$. No assumption on continuity of the targetwise weight choices was made in either shattering argument.

Write $H=L-2$ and let $U$ be its hidden unit count. Pad missing layers by empty layers if necessary. By [F1] and AM–GM, the restricted network has at most $M\le\prod_{\ell=1}^{H}(n_\ell+1)\le(1+U/H)^H$ affine intervals. One has length $h\ge1/M$. On this interval the network output $r$ is affine. If $g''\ge c_0$, midpoint convexity applied to $g(t)-c_0t^2/2$ gives $g(a)+g(b)-2g((a+b)/2)\ge c_0h^2/4$; in the other case apply this to $-g$. The affine second difference of $r$ is zero; the three uniform errors bound the absolute second difference of $g$ by $4\varepsilon$. Thus $\varepsilon\ge c_0/(16M^2)$. Rearranging gives $U\ge c(f,L)\varepsilon^{-1/(2H)}$ for small $\varepsilon$. Each hidden unit has a counted bias parameter, so the number of weights is at least $U$, proving clause (iii). AC and its countable-choice consequence are inherited through the stated Sobolev representative and width suppliers; the finite sign and segment constructions require no additional choice.
